newsitem.title: ITALY: Constitutional reform splits Italy's centre-right.
newsitem.headline: Constitutional reform splits Italy's centre-right.

text.p: Italy's centre-right opposition was divided on Tuesday over much-needed constitutional reforms, with smaller parties in the coalition resolutely opposed to an apparent opening by leader Silvio Berlusconi.
Former prime minister Berlusconi, who leads the Freedom Alliance bloc, told reporters that his centre-right was ready to discuss a two-round election with a runoff between the leading two groups.
"It is not beyond reason that the two leading coalitions should face off where they have not got 51 percent in the first round to obtain the necessary majority," he said.
Centre-right parties have already succeeded in getting backing at commission stage for a directly-elected president to govern alongside a parliamentary premier.
Berlusconi said the president should be given enhanced political powers, be able to dissolve parliament and name and fire a prime minister as well as ministers.
The ruling centre-left Olive Tree coalition instead wants to reinforce the powers of the prime minister and leave the president with a largely symbolic role, as is now the case.

Berlusconi was quoted in the daily Corriere della Sera on Tuesday as saying he was optimistic that the work of the cross-party commission looking into the much-needed reforms would achieve two main objectives:
"Fewer small parties and the possibility to govern for whoever wins," he was quoted as saying.

The small CDU and CCD parties in the Freedom Alliance which also includes Berlusconi's Forza Italia and his main far-right ally, the National Alliance, rejected his apparent backing for a system that could spell their political demise.
"None of us yet has a vocation for suicide," said CCD leader Pierferdinando Casini. "I didn't think even Berlusconi did. If he has changed his ideas, we have not."
Casini said the two-round system would ensure the left won for the next 20 years and warned coalition partners that marriages did not last without agreement.
Rocco Buttiglione, leader of the CDU, said that his party was against a two-round system.
"If others have good reasons we will listen to them. But I don't think there is a clear proposal on the field, in fact there is a lot of confusion."
Gianfranco Fini, the National Alliance leader, was optimistic an agreement was possible and backed a two-round option.

The reform commission, headed by the leader of the Democratic Party of the Left, Massimo d'Alema, must vote on proposals by June 30 before the agreed basic texts go before both houses of parliament for further debate.
Because they involve constitutional change, they must eventually go to a national referendum.
D'Alema warned last week that so many amendments had been put forward that voting on them all would be impossible.
The five basic texts cover the nature of the state, parliament, Europe, form of government and the judicial system.
The 70-member commission was set up earlier this year to map out constitutional reform in a bid to halt the revolving-door governments which have plagued Italy since World War Two.
Modern Italian governments have lasted just 11 months on average and Italy is now on its 55th since the war.
